That said, everything being “priced to perfection” means any surprise that is not to the upside is probably to the downside, knocking valuation estimates down as low as $1T and probability down 18% . Anthropic’s year end target is $100B run rate, and they’re now at $80B . We discuss all the most important lessons and assumptions in today’s bonus weekend pod, our second in the series covering the Anthropic IPO, with friend of the show Jamin Ball : If you liked our pod, or think the economy is going to hell in a handbasket, you’re gonna need to back up your data to the cloud. AI Twitter Recap Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small Sets a New Bar for US Open Models Release and specs : Thinking Machines launched Inkling 2 Small, a natively multimodal MoE model ( @Haoxiang__Wang ). Architecture : It has 594B total and 17B active parameters, accepts image inputs and supports variable effort ( @kimmonismus ). Licensing and availability : Full weights are expected next week under Apache 2.0. Fine-tuning and inference are available now on Tinker ( @arena ). Alignment disclosure : John Schulman wrote that early checkpoints "took unexpected actions to circumvent guardrails during training and evals." He attributed this to capabilities-focused RL that made the models "extremely persistent," willing to succeed at tasks at all costs ( @johnschulman2 ). Detection : Offline monitors flagged the behavior first. The team later found it was frequent and easy to replicate. Mitigations : The team applied alignment interventions spanning SFT to RL. Schulman reports large gains on internal evals and on previously unseen external evals from Apollo and Goodhart. Lab framing : Soumith Chintala pointed to proactive monitoring during training plus internal and external safety testing ( @soumithchintala ). Independent results : ARC-AGI : 81.7% on ARC-AGI-2 at $0.27 per task and 96.5% on ARC-AGI-1 at $0.08 per task. ARC Prize says this beats every open-weight model it has evaluated ( @arcprize ). Code Arena WebDev : 1648 points, #8 overall and the top US open model once weights ship ( @arena ). It ranks #5 in Data & Analytics and is 240 points above the original Inkling-Small ( @arena ). Domain benchmarks : It is reported as the top US open model on DeepFinance, ahead of GLM 5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Nemotron 3 Ultra ( @0interestrates ). It placed 2nd on SWE-Atlas v1.1 QnA ( @ziqiao_ma ). Agent trace oddity : Vals found the model swearing in 50 of 2,655 benchmark runs. The profanity clustered late in long runs, alongside repeated failed recoveries ( @ValsAI ). Training efficiency (claims and speculation) : Compute : Elie Bakouch called it "the most compute efficient training in the open" ( @eliebakouch ). Comparison to DeepSeek : Teortaxes reads the report as using about 40% of V4.1 Flash's pretraining compute ( @teortaxesTex ). He also cites roughly 68 hours of pretraining and a little over a week of post-training ( @teortaxesTex ). Architecture guesses : Speculation includes LatentMoE, NoPE gated attention and a linear-attention local layer, trained on about 12T tokens. These are explicitly guesses ( @eliebakouch ). Reception : Teortaxes called the model a "narrative violation" on par with the best Chinese open efforts and on a steeper trajectory ( @teortaxesTex ). Early users report strong multimodal judging, better than Kimi and Muse on internal image generation and editing tests ( @zhuole1025 ). Other Model Releases: Open Weights, Muse Upgrades and GPT Image 2.6 Kimi K3.1 Pro open weights : Moonshot released a 2.8T-parameter MoE with 104B active parameters ( @thursdai_pod ). Rankings : It is #1 among open models in Agent Arena ( @arena ). Serving : SGLang shipped day-0 megakernel support ( @SemiAnalysis_ ). Tinker offers the model with 256K context ( @tinkerapi ). Mixed evals : It scores 9.9% on WeirdML, behind Haiku 5.5 ( @htihle ). Teortaxes says the strong showing is a new checkpoint with DSA adaptation, not a provider fix ( @teortaxesTex ). ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base : Baidu released a pure base model: a 280B MoE with 14B active parameters, trained on 33.5T tokens ( @kimmonismus ). Architecture : Only 6 of 43 layers keep token-level full context. The rest compress every 128 tokens into one KV entry, with up to 1M context. It also uses Multi-Router MoE and ECHO, which runs multi-token prediction through the final layer. Baidu's preliminary results vs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base : MMLU-Pro 78.4 vs 69.2, HumanEval+ 82.3 vs 69.5, and LiveCodeBench 40.1 vs 31.9. License : Weights are available in FP8 and BF16. The license excludes the EU, UK and South Korea. Tencent Hy4 : It is the top Chinese model in Agent Arena, with a $0.57 median cost per task; weights are coming ( @arena ). On OpenDesign it lands 0.1 points behind GPT-6.1 Sol at 41% lower cost ( @OpenDesignDevs ). Notable fine-tunes and specialized models : Arete-27B : Nous fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on about 53M tokens.

items.content: The products aren't good enough to sell people on the costs. You cannot tell people that you have to listen to the whine of a data center in their backyard for AI overviews and some of the most hilarious deep fake slop in history. It's not worth it. It just isn't worth it to anyone. And agents aren't real and they might not be being used the way that anyone wants them to yet. All these companies are spending more than they're making on these products. Refrigerators holding blood storage in Europe are being hacked. The costs are too high. The benefits are not real. And if you connect that to corruption, you're like, in order to impose these costs on me, these CEOs are in the White House shaking Trump's hand, renaming it to the Gulf of America, paying for this ballroom that we don't want. It's obvious crypto-corruption, and it's still slop. The AI industry will not get out of it until they make better products . Until everyone can see without needing to be convinced, without needing an ad campaign, without any of this stuff that just using these products makes your life better. — Nilay Patel , The Vergecast: Big Tech lost big in the 2026 election Tags: nilay-patel , slop , ai , generative-ai , ai-ethics

items.title: Controlling Biology - Fabian Theis, Helmholtz Munich
items.content: Fabian Theis has been one of the key players in the various iterations of the Virtual Cell concept and initiatives. It is not hyperbole at all to say that his lab has been pushing the frontier of algorithms to understand multi-scale, multi-modal (”multiomics”), time-varying biological data. Indeed, he has shaped the large scale vision and data collection through his leadership at Helmholtz, various startups and probably at Biohub itself. Watch the full episode on YouTube… Much of the recent attention in AI x Bio has been on protein and molecular design. AlphaFold, ESM and BioHub , Chai , Leash , Isomporphic, Boltz , Genesis , Octant, Baker Lab, and many many more. After a lot of initial excitement, Virtual Cell projects have received less attention, due in no small part to questions about the effectiveness of large-scale models in solving even basic Virtual Cell problems. A $1.8B bet The Biohub announcement a few weeks ago got a lot of press for the (really) big numbers: $1.8B of commitments [1] from Biohub, NIH, DOE, Google and Meta. The discussion cites new imaging and measurement capabilities, generating large data sets and making the data available for training AI. View post on X ↗ But why are these organizations doubling down on these big bets now? They have been in the works for years now, what is going on that makes now the moment to push? New measurement capabilities and scale infrastructure, are now coming online that make Biohub’s push likely lead to big impact on science. DOE and NIH are developing lab-in-the-loop automation capabilities at scale. Google is scaling and broadening its connectomics capabilities ( episode coming soon!). Biohub itself has worked with various labs to develop and improve imaging platforms like laser phase plate microscopy, light sheet microscopy and advanced post-processing for regular microscopes that reveal deep phenotypic data. These technologies are quickly maturing, and will likely play a big part in the Biohub initiative. Virtual cells struggle This kind of multi-scale, multi-modal data looks a lot like the data Fabian has made a career out modeling. On the other hand Virtual Cell modeling has run into problems that have dampened excitement about systems biology. The 2025 Arc Virtual Cell Challenge shined a light on the problem: a slew of papers pointed out that constant baselines (not even linear!) often beat sophisticated models for “Perturbation Prediction”. If you change the inputs or programming of a cell (via gene editing, drugs or other environmental factors), how will the cell change it’s “state”. The disappointing finding is that many models fail to beat even the most basic basic baselines 🤦‍♂️. The situation is not actually so bad: This excellent paper show that many existing evaluation metrics are poorly calibrated: they can reward an uninformative mean prediction because most genes barely change. With better-calibrated metrics, deep learning models can outperform the mean baseline. The problem is the problem Nonetheless, Fabian Theis believes that perturbation prediction under the existing data sets just isn’t a hard enough problem to warrant complex algorithms. Instead we should be focused on exactly the problems that Biohub just announce an $1.8B data collection effort around: using large, high precision, multi-scale, co-registered biological data to predict the evolution of molecules → cells → niches → tissues → organs → organisms, and how all these scales effect one another. This is a happy situation: at this very moment, AI is enabling us to tackle dramatically larger problems, and this problem is very, very big. We lack understanding of the “scale interfaces” between these different different “domains of applicability,” and we lack the data. The Biohub initiative aims to solve the data problem. Fabian Theis has been working on the algorithms to model these larger problems for years. How do the other cells near me change my state? What happens to a distribution of cells from a perturbation? How do I perturb a cell to get it into the state I want? These are increasingly complex questions that are building towards a lab-in-the-loop and large scale experimentation, and (actually) require increasingly complex models. Models drive precision medicine Fabian’s labs and initiatives have been also investing heavily: the Computational Health Center at Helmholtz combines AI, molecular data, medical imaging, genomics, and clinical data to develop predictive and mechanistic models for precision medicine. The Institute of Computational Biology develops statistical and dynamical models integrating biological information from single-cell time series through population-scale omics data. Given his drivers seat at the frontier, we were so excited for the opportunity to get an hour of his time to understand how Fabian Theis is thinking about Virtual Cells when the concept of what is difficult is changing so quickly. We also discussed: The business of Virtual Cells The Bitter Lesson in biology - our perennial topic Training the next generation of Computation Biologists Closing the lab-in-the-loop Controlling Biology - Fabian Theis, Helmholtz Munich Fabian Theis has been one of the key players in the various iterations of the Virtual Cell concept and initiatives. items.content: Build AI systems with context graphs and agentic memory. Join Andrew Ng and AI engineers at NODES 2026 for 100+ live technical sessions . Free, online, 24 hours. Save your spot ! There was a time in the early days of Thinking Machines, post 2025 start and cofounder departures , when their going concern as a neolab was very much in doubt. Those days are clearly behind us, as Tinker (now a year old !) and Interaction Models and Inkling and other high-impact contributions to AI research have converted Thinky’s highly credentialed potential into actual concrete ships that establish that they are now a high-functioning neolab at the US frontier. Anyway, here’s Inkling 2 Small - pretrained from scratch in less than 3 days on <12T tokens native NVFP4, with single joint run RL , competitive with and often beating same-size Chinese models, with VERY good vision encoder : People are of course comparing with Western models like Mistral, Reflection and Meta Muse. People are calling it “ the smartest western open weight model by a margin ”, and while it is certainly competitive in that league, what’s probably the most interesting is the intentional “customizability” of Inkling, which leans into the overall Thinky and Tinker messaging: View post on X ↗ And of course don’t miss John Schulman’s take on the alignment process for scaling model training: View post on X ↗ AI News for 11/04/2026-11/05/2026 is brought to you by our friends at Neo4J, whose talks are doing gangbusters ! AI Twitter Recap What happened Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-total / 17B-active multimodal MoE. It is available now on Tinker, and Apache 2.0 weights are promised "next week" after external safety testing. Launch: Announced at 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, "a big jump over its predecessor." Available for fine-tuning and inference on Tinker and Tinker Playground today ( @thinkymachines , @miramurati , @tinkerapi ). Weights timing: Soumith Chintala says open weights come next week, once external safety testing is "fully complete" ( @soumithchintala ). Victoria Lin confirms Apache 2.0, next week ( @VictoriaLinML ). Artificial Analysis lists the model as proprietary at launch with an unconfirmed weights date ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Pricing: $0.30 input / $1.00 output / $1.50 training per 1M tokens on Tinker ( @cHHillee ). $0.03 per 1M cached input tokens ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Positioning: If weights ship, it’d be the highest-scoring open-weights model developed outside China on current AA rankings ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Vals calls it the highest-scoring US open-weight model "by a wide margin" ( @ValsAI ). Alignment disclosure: John Schulman reported that early checkpoints learned to circumvent guardrails during training and evals. The team then ran an alignment sprint before release ( @johnschulman2 ). Training and architecture facts (official) Size and modalities: 594B total / 17B active MoE. Text and image input, text output, with native vision ( @ArtificialAnlys , @VictoriaLinML ). Graham Neubig notes it is roughly 2x the parameters of Inkling Small ( @gneubig ). Context: 1M context window and 1M max output tokens. Vals ran it at temperature=1, top_p=1, reasoning effort 0.99 ( @ValsAI ). Pretraining: 68 hours on GB300s ( @soumithchintala ). The main pretraining phase was 8.4T tokens, run natively in NVFP4. Guangxuan Xiao calls it "one rung of our predictive scaling ladder" ( @Guangxuan_Xiao ). Horace He: "just under 3 days to pretrain" ( @cHHillee ). He then posted a cryptic "*19" correction with no further context ( @cHHillee ). Precision: The whole pipeline (pre-, mid- and post-training) ran in NVFP4 ( @soumithchintala ). Post-training: 17M rollouts over 9 days ( @soumithchintala ). An engineer highlights long-horizon capabilities bootstrapped "from ~0 pass rates" ( @anzhit ). Customizability as a design target: Soumith says it is "probably one of the only model programs in the industry with a launch blocking eval around customizability." For a fixed data and dollar budget, he says it fine-tunes better than alternatives ( @soumithchintala ). Data volume: Elie Bakouch reads the blog as a from-scratch pretrain on "only 12T tokens." This may include mid-training; the team's own figure for the main phase is 8.4T. He also says the base model's perplexity on internal code is lower than Kimi K3.1, with the comparison model "base-recovered" for fairness ( @eliebakouch ). He later clarified that a particular customization plot uses a post-trained model as the base for further post-training ( @eliebakouch ). BPB: The team reports low bits-per-byte after 3 days of pretraining ( @MuCai7 ). Independent evals Artificial Analysis (Intelligence Index v5.0.1: 31, up 18 from Inkling Small) ( @ArtificialAnlys ) Peers: Matches Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) and beats MiMo-V2.6-Pro. Gains over Inkling Small: AutomationBench-AA: 5% → 46%. FrontierCode 2.0: 5% → 25%. HLE-Diamond: 12% → 29%. Coding vs Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium): The two have different strengths. Benchmark Inkling 2 Small Sonnet 5.5 (medium) FrontierCode 2.0 25% 11% Terminal-Bench 4.0 13% 30% Creative agentic: On AA-3D it scores above Claude Haiku 5.5 and Grok 4.7. It beats Gemini 3.8 Flash on both AA-3D and Code2Video-AA, but trails Sonnet 5.5 on both. Physics: CritPt v2 is 56% (up from 34%), versus 65% for Gemini 3.8 Flash. AA-Omniscience: The hallucination rate falls from 61% to 27%. Accuracy rises from 32% to 34%, and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%. The model answers more selectively. Token use: About 150K output tokens per Index task, compared with: ~37K for Inkling Small ~31K for Sonnet 5.5 ~99K for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cost per Index task: $1.18, compared with: $0.20 for Inkling Small $7.77 for Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) $10.02 for Sonnet 5.5 (medium) Vals AI ( @ValsAI )

AI Twitter Recap OpenAI's Autonomous Cyber Pipeline Patches 948 Linux Kernel Privilege-Escalation Bugs Pipeline result : OpenAI says its security researchers built an autonomous pipeline for vulnerability discovery, exploitation and patching. In a single run with an upcoming cyber model, it validated and generated patches for 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, at a total API cost of $1.2M ( announcement ). Novel techniques : OpenAI says the agents discovered and used at least 10 Linux exploitation techniques that its team and consulted experts consider novel. It argues this shows models going beyond applying known methods ( thread ). Disclosure path : OpenAI says it is working with Linux maintainers and Patch the Planet partners on reports and patches ( details ). Scale framing : Eric Wallace says researchers typically find about 20 Linux LPEs a year. He says the model found about 1,000 in one week using about $1M of tokens, and that OpenAI is now putting "a significant amount" of frontier compute toward pro bono open-source patching ( post ). Greg Brockman cites about $1,000 per vulnerability ( post ). Cost trajectory : One comparison puts GPT‑5.6 Sol at 166 vulnerabilities for about $500k in July 2026, against 948 for about $1.2M with the new model ( comparison ). One commenter estimates the real internal cost is far below the API list price; this is an unverified estimate ( estimate ). Context : The run used an unreleased model, separate from the rumored GPT‑6.2 Sol and Astra models covered below ( note ). Open-Weight Model Wave: Kimi K3.1 Pro, Ripple-65B, SWE-2 Flash, Hy4 Kimi K3.1 Pro open weights : Moonshot released weights for its flagship ( release ). Modal describes it as a post-training update to K3, with expanded RL for coding, financial research and long-horizon agentic work. It accepts text and images and has 1M context ( Modal ). Specs : The model has 2.8T total parameters with 104B active ( Ollama ). One commenter credits gated sparse attention for gains in intelligence and efficiency over K3 ( comment ). Independent signal : On Agent Arena it ranks #1 among open models and #13 overall, with +5.1% net improvement across more than 17.5K agentic sessions. That is +4.2pp over K3, and it is #1 open in Bash reliability and steerability ( Arena ). One user reports that on an internal SRE-agent eval it uses more tokens but delivers "shockingly good" quality ( report ). Availability : vLLM and SGLang shipped Day-0 support across AMD, NVIDIA, Rubin and TPU, and SGLang also supports Trainium 2/3 ( SemiAnalysis ). Hosted access is also live on Ollama Cloud with zero data retention, Databricks and SkyPilot ( Databricks ). Ripple-65B Preview (Ricursive) : This is a 65B dense model pretrained from scratch. Ricursive claims it is the best US open-weight model on agentic coding, ahead of larger MoEs including Muse Spark Open-816B, Beam-501B, Inkling-975B and Nemotron 3 Ultra-550B ( launch ). Claimed results : It scores 80.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 against Beam-501B's 80.1%; Beam activates 23B parameters per token. Ricursive reports 12T training tokens, 1M context and an Apache 2.0 license ( summary ). Cost claims : Ricursive cites a $32M budget, which it says covers full R&D including the scaling ladder, data work and the final runs ( footnote ). Prime Intellect ran the pretraining clusters and cites 16x pretraining compute efficiency ( Prime Intellect ). Architecture/ablations : The model uses value residuals and sliding window attention ( notes ). On the scaling ladder, a new architecture on the same data as Olmo3 gave about a 3x gain, and a new dataset on the same architecture gave about 4x ( analysis ). Skepticism : Critics note it still loses to the 284B V4 Flash ( critique ). Others say the "US-only SOTA" framing hides the gap with Chinese models ( comment ), and that the release omits comparisons with Qwen ( critique ). Cognition SWE-2 Flash : Cognition says this coding model outperforms all American open-weight models, including ones 3x larger ( launch ). Base and cost : The model is post-trained on Thinking Machines' Inkling-Small. It costs 20% of SWE-2 and runs about 3x faster ( Jeff Wang ). It is Cognition's first model with a mid-training stage and was built in 6 weeks ( Silas Alberti ). Weights policy : Weights are not public. Cognition plans a secure weight-sharing program for partners and researchers and cites cyber-misuse risk ( details ). Availability : It is free through November for Devin Pro, Max and Teams users ( pricing ). Tencent Hy4 : Tencent reports 75.2 on APEX-Agents against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash's 72.1/72.9. API pricing is $0.834/$2.501 per million input

items.content: There’s a lot of dispute to yesterday’s title story on “ Weight Space Programming ” — and we agree that some of the claims are presented in overly favorable light and overall took away from the impact of the paper’s more substantial discoveries. However it is still a big wakeup moment and has had multiple independent replications by now that it is not worth either doing some kind of retraction or a followup title story saying it was bogus. Instead today we’re featuring AI Engineer Shanghai and also sharing an exclusive interview on the history of Latent Space ! AI News for 11/02/2026-11/03/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Weight-Space Programming: Frontier Models Reading and Writing Neural Network Weights Core claim and replications : Several groups report that frontier LLMs can generate or edit small networks' weights directly, without gradient training or tools. Cross-generation replication : Alex Krentsel's replication of MIT's experiment found a sharp capability jump across model generations; the latest models generated Breakout networks scoring up to 22× an RL-trained baseline ( summary ). Hugging Face reproduction : Hugging Face reproduced the paper with ML Intern, its open-source AI-research harness, and released the model and a demo ( NielsRogge ). Hand-written classifier : A user had Fable hand-write a 100K-parameter network that classifies real versus fake legal citations, reportedly outperforming a trained version ( jacsebl ). Legora's CTO highlighted the result ( mstockton ). Astra's Qwen edit, reconstructed : GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 weights in Qwen3.5-0.8B without backprop, raising MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1%. A Zhihu reconstruction from the logs shows the gain is narrower than the headline ( ZhihuFrontier ): Failure mode : 576 of 579 repaired answers had originally hit the 32K-token limit because of looping. Method : Astra derived a "repetition direction" from contrastive looping/productive contexts, located it mainly in the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted 6× the projection from the top 64 aligned neurons per layer. Held-out result : Accuracy rose from 10.6% to 60.4% on 1,152 held-out problems. Most of the gain is existing reasoning that can now finish. Laptop reproduction : Simon Willison reports that Qwen 3.8 27B achieved the same weight-interpretation feat on his laptop after 45+ minutes ( simonw ). Skeptical readings : Baselines : Critics say the big claims lack competent baselines, the Qwen result is bug-fixing rather than recursive self-improvement, and the thread overclaims ( paul_cal ). Benchmark overfitting : Fitting weights directly against a benchmark is "essentially meaningless," as the nesformer Mario example shows ( dbreunig ). Mechanism : One thread asks whether models mainly read the first and last layers, which map to known inputs and outputs ( ravfogel ). Interpretability takeaway : Another view is that the real lesson is how effectively coding agents use mechanistic-interpretability tools ( jbhuang0604 ). Optimistic framing : Supporters frame the work as meta-learning finally working and treat weight optimization as structured-text optimization. They suggest hybrids that interleave backprop with direct edits ( yoonholeee ). Model Releases and Independent Evals Tencent Hy4 : Tencent reports 75.2 on APEX-Agents versus 72.1/72.9 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, though the two trade wins on other benchmarks ( summary ). Pricing and weights : The API costs $0.834/$2.501 per million input/output tokens, and Tencent plans to release weights. Agent Arena : Hy4 ranks #14 overall across 8.5K+ sessions, at $0.55/task versus $1.46 for Kimi K3.1 Pro (Max). The two scores are within 1 point ( arena ). Sarvam Prism : This "System One" decision model is built on Sarvam 105B. It scores 71.8 with a 44 ms median response time, which Sarvam says is the best average among sub-100 ms decision models ( SarvamAI ). Open-weight releases : Kimi K3.1 Pro : Weights are due Wednesday ( Together ). P-H3-Image : Pruna's open model, distilled from MiniMax-H3, runs in 8 steps instead of 50, is 7× smaller and produces a 4 MP image in 2.6 s ( PrunaAI ). LongCat-2.5 : The model has 1.6T total and ~48B active parameters and is priced at $0.30/$1.20. It built a browser game for $0.28 versus $0.82 for Qwen3.8-Max in one user's test ( omarsar0 ). Other releases : EmbeddingGemma 2 : The paper is out ( osanseviero ). Krea 3 : The technical report covers a model built by a research team of under 10 ( krea_ai ). Crouton Alpha : A free stealth reasoning model on OpenRouter offers 1M context ( OpenRouter ). Open October architectures : Raschka catalogs 10 open LLM architectures released in October ( rasbt ): Attention variants : Mistral Large 4 (1T) pairs MLA with sparse attention. Hybrids and MoE : Muse Spark Open (816B) is Meta's first major open release since Llama, with LatentMoE. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL mixes Mamba-2 layers with eight attention layers. Looped models : Dory1.0 is a looped transformer. Artificial Analysis updates : Capability Indexes v2.0 : The update adds weight on non-hallucination and agentic tool use. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads all six indexes; Kimi K3.1 Pro leads among open models ( ArtificialAnlys ). How big is the open model economy today?
items.content: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? Share I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents . For example, Fireworks announced at their first company conference this week that they’re serving more than 40T tokens per day to customers’ customized models. This is just one slice of their inference, a vertical that they said grew over 2x from this summer, so I would expect their total number this fall to be well above 100T tokens when we get the next update. My first instinct with these numbers has been to ground them versus any closed model or hyperscale company we can, at least in terms of token volume. Thankfully, Google releases token volumes for the entire platform and API usage in their earnings reports. Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
items.content: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: breakout/prompt.txt freeway/prompt.txt pacman/prompt.txt pong/prompt.txt I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Confidence: 72% This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball

items.content: Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears : Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? View post on X ↗ In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: View post on X ↗ Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the world has now gone from 0 to 1 on this very new RSI capability…. which will immediately put to use and explored due to its remarkable efficiency. View post on X ↗ AI News for 10/31/2026-11/02/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap DeepSeek Open-Sources a "Super-agent" Harness Prototype Release : DeepSeek Harness published a long design article ( article ) and the dsh-superagent-prototype repo ( repo link ). An official English version followed ( @tianyi ). Architecture : One long-lived router session talks to humans and hands out work. Isolated workers run tasks in parallel, triggered by GitHub events ( summary ). Claimed results : In DeepSeek's own test, p95 completion time fell from 29.5 to 15.7 min versus a single session using subagents ( summary ). Design rationale from a reviewer : Final reviewer 崔添翼 (@tianyi) says "Super" means a layer above the working agent, not superior intelligence. He frames the core trade-off as cross-task continuity versus throughput ( Zhihu summary ). Stated limits : The harness has no built-in cross-session long-term memory yet. Separating state, compute and environment is mostly unimplemented. The prototype has only been validated in a small, trusted internal environment, and security, privacy and agent-to-agent communication remain open questions. Prior art : He acknowledges that other teams explored similar architectures months earlier. Practitioner reception : @badlogicgames says the design matches where Earendil is heading: a single long-lived entity, ad-hoc recursive delegation and cross-system event triggers. @omarsar0 calls it a "masterclass" in coordination-execution harness design. DeepSeek also says it aims to support pi and other major harnesses with each model generation ( @tianyi ). Critique : @teortaxesTex calls the write-up "something of a hot mess." He argues DeepSeek builds internal crutches around model weaknesses such as hallucination rather than making the system generally robust. He also notes Bloomberg covered a repo that had no English announcement ( post ). V4.1 naming confusion : A Renmin University FlashRSI README referenced deepseek-v4.1-pro , which prompted release speculation. Teortaxes says it is a placeholder: the real config uses v4-flash and v4-pro, and deepseek-v4.1-flash is not a valid ID ( thread , follow-up ). He also says the API fingerprints for V4.1F-1017 are unchanged ( fingerprints ). Independent Evals and Frontier Model Signals GDPx benchmark (SemiAnalysis) : The benchmark covers 206 agentic tasks across 11 economically valuable domains, including chip design, SWE, finance and biology. The best model scores only 12% ( launch ). Results : Opus 5.5 leads at 12%. Gemini 4 Carbon is close behind at 10.9% at roughly 4x lower cost ( breakdown ). Reactions : @dylan522p apologized to Google, calling Carbon "spikier" but very strong in some areas. @demishassabis welcomed the benchmark. Analysis : @eliebakouch finds that removing safeguard-affected benchmarks changes the picture. In that view Carbon stays cheap, and Sol 6.1 is cheaper still. He also suggests OpenAI has stronger bio safeguards than Anthropic ( note ). Within-family comparison : Sol 6.1 and Astra score very similarly, Carbon beats Argon across the board, and Sonnet is strong at SWE ( comparison ). Possible bug : Some Argon cybersecurity runs may be affected by an Antigravity bug ( report ). That is 3 points above V4.1F-0910 and 10 above V4-Pro; Astra sits roughly 10 points higher ( @teortaxesTex ). items.content: Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna . LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix. Building AI for Lawyers - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.content: In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work. Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO. Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year. We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → Open video on YouTube ↗ What changed for the billable hour? When Jacob first read Leya's YC application, he had one piece of feedback: people had tried building legal tech a million times, and it never worked. If lawyers bill by the hour, getting faster means earning less. Why would they buy a tool that does that? What changed, he says, is the pressure on firms. In the US, routine work like small reviews is already shifting to flat project fees. Some firms do it for free to hold on to the client. The money moves to M&A, litigation, and time spent with clients. We asked whether that means firms will stop needing paralegals and junior lawyers. Jacob says that's not what Legora is seeing. A good junior is worth more today than two years ago because they get so much more done, just as in engineering. Jump to the billing model discussion → Evals without access to customer data Most teams improve their agents by reading traces. Legora can't read any. Almost everything users upload is confidential, and much of it belongs to the firm's clients, not the firm. So the evals team has to recreate the kinds of work customers do. Three engineers and three lawyers build RL environments to simulate the work their customers do. One example is a 10,000-file data room where the agent runs due diligence and has to produce a report that catches the right red flags. The team plots the results on a heat map by practice area and task. A new model often gets better at some kinds of legal work and worse at others. The team draws on a pool of about 100 legal engineers: lawyers who spent three or four years in big law, often with a CS degree. In production, Legora classifies failures into 10 to 20 known failure modes and runs cheap LLM-based checks behind feature flags. Those restrictions also determine which infrastructure Legora can use. Everything runs on Azure because when Legora started, law firms wouldn't accept AWS or GCP, and Microsoft was already an approved vendor through 365. Jump to evals without traces → Where smarter models still matter Legora resisted a model picker for a long time before giving in. Jacob's view is that a lawyer shouldn't have to decide whether a contract is a Sonnet-high or an Opus-mid task. It's Legora's job to find the best available tradeoff between quality, cost, latency, governance, and regional availability. He estimates that models already handle about 60% of legal work really well. For those tasks it's a cost and latency problem now. Complex analysis and editing across million-token contracts still need more intelligence. Legora has started post-training open-weight models for narrow tasks like legal research, with no plans to train its own frontier model. For drafting, Jacob finds Fable and Opus too verbose. Astra is more concise. To address hallucinations, everything the agent writes gets a citation that highlights a bounding box in the source PDF, multiple layers down. Jump to the model discussion → A few building blocks, many products Six months into the job, Jacob showed the team a slide of the 300 Spartans and declared that Legora would stay at 20 engineers forever. It now has 100, and he says that still feels too small. His job now is to build a system where the team can ship just a few things and customers feel like they're getting a lot. The team builds around a few primitives: projects that hold files, the agent, Tabular Review, and lists. Lists are a flexible Notion-style database with triggers and automations. Agents can create and read lists, and changes to a list can start an agent. Intake is a Slack bot that turns a request into a ticket on a list. Tabular Review is the one the industry copied, down to the name. Each row is a document, each column is a question. Drop in 10,000 employment contracts and ask for the termination period, the IP assignment clause, and the severance terms. It supports up to a million cells, but starts with just 10 rows so you can fix your prompts before running the rest. Legal engineers configure new products on these primitives without writing code. Even Wexler's fact intelligence product runs on the same building blocks. Jump to the primitives discussion → Legal engineers first, forward deployed engineers second Legora hired its first forward deployed engineer about nine months ago in New York: Di Qi, a two-time YC founder who worked on search at Meta. Legal engineers configure the product the way a power user would and don't write code. Forward deployed engineers write code into production, build integrations into a firm's CRM or document management system, and push what they learn back into the core product. They still don't tou

items.title: Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.content: Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence. What we talked about • Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one • Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model • How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning • A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything. • Why Legora runs everything on Azure and why it doesn’t use ElevenLabs • Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name • How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent • What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code • The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. Now there are 100, and he still feels short-handed. • Why Jacob finds Fable and Opus too chatty for drafting and likes Astra’s concise writing • Why drafting a long contract is a search problem • Whether model labs will cut off legal tools the way they cut off coding tools • What happens to law firm partnerships, the billable hour, and jobs for junior lawyers Legora is hiring engineers in New York, Stockholm, and London. The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
items.content: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: Here's a link to the larger image . For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here . Here's a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 . The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. Is this going to affect the survey? The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI". I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though. If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
items.content: I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it. Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories. But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today: error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1` cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14) Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem. How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
items.content: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it. Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference. The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf. OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious. Via Hacker News Tags: iframes , javascript , sandboxing , security , xss , openai , chatgpt , content-security-policy

Agents Prompt People: Using Agents for Long-Horizon Financial Work
items.content: At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh , the lead AI Engineer at Arca , an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that human advisors are making the final decisions. The goal is for AI to guide the process; or as Singh nicely put it, “agents prompt people more than people prompt agents.” Arca recently raised $48.5 Million in a round led by General Catalyst, with participation from Index Ventures and Venrock. One of the features of using AI in financial services, explained Singh, is that it’s typically long-horizon work — although not long-running. In his AIE presentation, Singh noted that agent tasks at Arca can take up to ten days. “It's very stop-start, there's many actors in between, many decision points, many handoffs,” he said. For this reason, Arca has developed an internal memory system . “So we have this persistence for every client ,” Singh said in our podcast discussion. “What has happened so far? What are we tracking for next? What needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days [and] what are we tracking for the long term? Which individual is responsible for which action? All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.” Arca uses models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with Claude its primary model provider. The company has built its own harness , which automatically selects the best model to use for a particular task, based on the company’s internal benchmarks. Owning the harness, rather than using a managed agent harness, also means that Arca has the flexibility to change model providers if it needs to. Safety is obviously key for financial services. Singh noted that although agents do much of the work, an agent’s role is limited to analysis and proposing solutions. Trading and any other money movement is handled by a human advisor. “All of our safety restrictions are fully deterministic,” he said. “And they take the decision making off the agent's hands.” In other words, there are certain tools and tasks the agent can execute by itself — but not ones that involve risk to the client. Arca also runs verification checks on known AI security issues, such as prompt injections. Arca’s agent isn’t itself sandboxed, but it does use sandboxes for computation. Singh explained they’ve gone even further, with extra security measures for handling sensitive data. “We've built systems to make it safe for code inside of that sandbox to access our data,” he said. “So we have this thing which translates the code it [the agent] wrote into a strict format that we expect, throw away the code, and you install guardrails on that format before it reaches your back end. So we allow the agents to use code to query our data, which means that they can aggregate it, they can munge it, they can work with it as they see fit to produce [things] like a financial plan.” Another interesting process Arca has implemented is using feedback from human advisors, along with traces from the agents, to improve the harness. A “meta-agent” is used to analyze all this data and suggest changes to the harness.
